where $\overline{L}_{i}=\pi_{i}^{*}\overline{L}_{\Phi}$ and $\overline{L}_{\Phi}$ is the $\Phi$ -invariant adelic line bundle satisfying $\Phi^{*}\overline{L}_{\Phi}=d^{m}\overline{L}_{\Phi}$ . Then by the projection formula, the numerator is $(d^{m}+1)^{\dim V+1}\widehat{h}_{\Phi}(\Phi_{m}(V))$ and so we obtain

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi}(\Phi_{m}(V))=(d^{m}+1)\widehat{h}_{\Phi}(V). $$

∎

We now need the following application of arithmetic Bézout [9]. For a point $x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ , we define its $\ell_{2}$ -height as

$$ h_{2}\left(x\right)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\log\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{v} $$

where $\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{v}=\max\left\{\left|x_{0}\right|_{v},\left|x_{1}\right|_{v}\right\}$ for non-archimedean $v$ and is $\sqrt{\left|x_{0}\right|^{2}+\left|x_{1}\right|^{2}}$ for archimedean $v$ . We have the inequalities $h\left(x\right)\leq h_{2}\left(x\right)\leq h\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log 2$ .

#### Proposition 8.3.

Let $z_{0}\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ and let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{k}$ be an irreducible subvariety. Let $V_{z_{0}}=V\cap\left\{z_{k}=z_{0}\right\}$ where we represent a point on $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{k}$ as $\left(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}\right)$ . Then

$$ \deg\left(V_{z_{0}}\right)\leq\deg V\text{ and }h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V_{z_{0}}\right)\leq h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)+\left(\deg V\right)h_{2}\left(z_{0}\right) $$

where $h_{\operatorname{Ph}}$ denotes the Philippon height.

#### Proof.

The Segre embedding $\iota:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{k}\to\mathbb{P}^{2^{k}-1}$ corresponds to sending

$$ ([x_{1}:y_{1}],[x_{2}:y_{2}],\ldots,[x_{n},y_{n}])\mapsto(\prod_{i\in I}x_{i}\prod_{i\not\in I}y_{i})_{I} $$

where we vary over all subsets $I$ of $\{1,2,\ldots,k\}$ . By composing with an automorphism of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , we may assume that $z_{0}\not=\infty$ . Then the hyperplane $\{z_{k}=z_{0}\}$ corresponds to $\{x_{k}=z_{0}y_{k}\}$ . Under the Segre embedding, if $J$ is any subset of $\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\}$ ¡ then we obtain the relation $X_{J\cup n}=z_{0}X_{J}.$ Furthermore, if we intersect the image of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{k}$ with $X_{J\cup\{k\}}=z_{0}X_{J}$ over all $J$ , we obtain back $x_{k}=z_{0}y_{k}$ . Hence $\iota(V_{z_{0}})$ can be viewed as $\iota(V)$ intersected with $2^{k-1}$ many hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}^{2^{k}-1}$ , each of height $h_{2}(z_{0})$ .

We now apply [72, Proposition 3.3]. Since $\dim V_{z_{0}}\geq\dim V-1$ , we obtain $\deg(V_{z_{0}})\leq\deg V$ and $h_{\operatorname{Ph}}(V_{z_{0}})\leq h_{\operatorname{Ph}}(V)+(\deg V)h(z_{0})$ as desired. ∎

We are now ready to prove a dynamical height gap principle for non-preperiodic hypersurfaces $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ . We define

$$ h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f_{i}\right). $$

#### Proposition 8.4.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and each $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. Let $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be a hypersurface of degree $D$ that is not weakly $\Phi$ -special. Then there exists $c=c\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)\geq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.5.

We proceed by induction on $n$ . When $n=2$ , at least one map is non-exceptional, so the two definitions of weakly special agree and Theorem 7.2 applies. Suppose that $n\geq 3$ . After rearranging coordinates, let $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(f_{1})$ be maximal and choose the last coordinate so that $\Phi^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1})$ still contains a non-exceptional map. This is possible since $n\geq 3$ , and we have

$$ h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\Phi^{\prime})\geq h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(f_{1})\geq\frac{1}{n}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\Phi). $$

Let $\pi_{n}:H\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be the projection to the last coordinate. For each $z\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ , we let $H_{z}$ denote the fiber $\pi_{n}^{-1}\left(z\right)$ . Let $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ be the projection to the first $n-1$ coordinates. Then $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ is a union of hypersurfaces in $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ . Let $O_{f_{n}}^{-}\left(1\right)$ denote the backward orbit of $1$ , i.e. $\cup_{m=1}^{\infty}\left(f_{n}\right)^{-m}\left(1\right)$ . We call a hypersurface a cylinder if it is the inverse image of a hypersurface under a projection forgetting one coordinate.

#### Lemma 8.5.

There exists only finitely many $z\in O_{f_{n}}^{-}\left(1\right)$ so that every irreducible component of $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ is weakly $\Phi^{\prime}$ -special for $\Phi^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1})$ .

#### Proof.

First, if there are only infinitely many $z\in O_{f_{n}}^{-}\left(1\right)$ so that $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ is preperiodic, then each such $H_{z}$ has a Zariski dense set of points with canonical height $\leq\widehat{h}_{f_{n}}(z)$ . In particular, it follows that $H$ has a Zariski dense set of small points. Since $H$ is not a cylinder, it projects dominantly onto every collection of $n-1$ coordinates. By [47, Theorem 2.2], together with [67], every $f_{i}$ would then be exceptional, contradicting our hypothesis.

Next, we assume that we have infinitely many $z$ such that $(\pi^{\prime})^{-1}(W_{z})$ is a component of $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ for some projection $\pi^{\prime}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n-1}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n-2}$ . Let $Z$ be this set of $z$ ’s. Then $W_{z}$ is a hypersurface in $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-2}$ and after rearranging coordinates, we may write $H_{z}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times W_{z}\times\{z\}$ . Let $\psi:H\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ be the projection from the first coordinate. Then for $x\in W_{z}\times\{z\}$ , we have $\psi^{-1}(x)=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{x\}$ .

Let $W$ be the Zariski closure of $\cup_{z\in Z}(W_{z}\times\{z\})$ . Then $W\subseteq\psi(H)$ with $\dim W\geq n-2$ . Note that for $w\in W$ , we must have $\psi^{-1}(w)=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{w\}$ since it is true for a dense set of points. Then $\dim\psi^{-1}(W)\geq n-1$ and in particular we must have $\psi^{-1}(W)=H$ which contradicts $H$ being non-weakly special.

Finally if there exists infinitely many $z$ such that a component of $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ does not project dominantly to one of the coordinates, after rearranging coordinates there must be infinitely many such $z$ so that a component of $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ is equal to $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-2}\times\left\{w_{z}\right\}$ and so is of the form $\pi^{-1}_{n-1}\left(w_{z}\right)$ . This is covered by the previous case and so we are done here too. ∎

Now let $Z$ be the subset of $O_{f_{n}}^{-}\left(1\right)$ so that all irreducible component of $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ are weakly $\Phi^{\prime}$ -special for $z\in Z$ . Since $\pi\left(H_{z}\right)$ is not weakly $\Phi^{\prime}$ -special for $z\not\in Z$ , we may apply induction. Let $\Phi^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1})$ so that $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi^{\prime}\right)\geq\frac{1}{n}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right)$ since $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(f_{1})$ is maximal. Then by induction, we have a constant $c^{\prime}=c^{\prime}\left(d,n-1,D\right)$ so that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi^{\prime}}\left(\pi\left(H_{z}\right)\right)\geq c^{\prime}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi^{\prime}\right),1\right\}\geq\frac{c^{\prime}}{n}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}. $$

Note that $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H_{z}\right)\geq\widehat{h}_{\Phi^{\prime}}\left(\pi\left(H_{z}\right)\right)$ and so we have a lower bound $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H_{z}\right)\geq\frac{c^{\prime}}{n}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}$ for $z\not\in Z$ .

For $m\geq 1$ , we now consider $\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\cap F$ for $F=\left\{z_{2n}=1\right\}$ where we let $z_{1},\ldots,z_{2n}$ be the coordinates for $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2n}$ . By Proposition 8.3, we have

$$ h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\cap F\right)\leq h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)+\left(\deg\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)\left(\log 2\right). $$

On the other hand, for $z$ satisfying $f_{n}^{m}\left(z\right)=1$ , we have that $\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)$ correspond to a finite union of irreducible components of $\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\cap F$ . Furthermore different $z$ ’s correspond to disjoint components. Hence we have

$$ \sum_{f_{n}^{m}\left(z\right)=1}h\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right)\leq h\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\cap F\right)\leq h\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)+\left(\deg\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)\left(\log 2\right) $$

We now change the Philippon heights to normalized canonical heights using (2.1). First, note that

$$ \deg\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right)=\left(d^{m}+1\right)^{\dim H-1}\deg\left(H_{z}\right)\geq\left(d^{m}+1\right)^{\dim H-1} $$

and

$$ \deg\left(h\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)\right)=\left(d^{m}+1\right)^{\dim H}\left(\deg H\right). $$

Hence

$$ \frac{1}{\deg\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)}\sum_{f^{m}_{n}\left(z\right)=1}h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right)\geq\frac{1}{\left(d^{m}+1\right)\deg H}\sum_{f^{m}_{n}\left(z\right)=1}\widehat{h}_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right) $$

and so we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{\left(d^{m}+1\right)\deg H}\sum_{f^{m}_{n}\left(z\right)=1}\widehat{h}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right)\leq\widehat{h}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)+\log 2. $$

We may then change from $\widehat{h}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)$ to $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)$ and occur a constant error $c_{1}=c_{1}\left(\Phi\right)$ which depends only on $\Phi$ by (2.1). Hence

$$ \frac{1}{\left(d^{m}+1\right)\deg H}\sum_{f^{m}_{n}\left(z\right)=1}\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H_{z}\right)\right)\leq\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)+\left(c_{1}+\log 2\right). $$

Now since $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(\Phi_{m}\left(H\right)\right)=\left(d^{m}+1\right)\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)$ and similarly for $H_{z}$ , we get

$$ \frac{1}{\left(d^{m}+1\right)\deg H}\sum_{f^{m}_{n}\left(z\right)=1}\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H_{z}\right)\leq\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)+\frac{1}{d^{m}+1}\left(c_{1}+\log 2\right). $$

Since $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H_{z}\right)\geq\frac{c^{\prime}}{n}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}$ for all $z\not\in Z$ , we obtain

$$ \frac{d^{m}-\left|Z\right|}{\left(d^{m}+1\right)\deg H}\frac{c^{\prime}}{n}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}\leq\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)+\frac{1}{d^{m}+1}\left(c_{1}+\log 2\right). $$

As $\left|Z\right|$ is finite, taking $M\to\infty$ gives us $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)\geq\frac{c^{\prime}}{n\deg H}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}$ which completes the induction.

∎

Applying Theorem 2.1, we immediately deduce the following corollary.

#### Corollary 8.6.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at least one $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. Let $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible hypersurface of degree $D$ that is not weakly $\Phi$ -special. Then there exists $c=c\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ and $E=E\left(d,n,D\right)$ such that

$$ \left\{x\in H\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)\mid\widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(x\right)\leq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}\right\} $$

is contained in a proper Zariski closed subvariety $V$ of degree at most $E$ .

#### Proof.

After conjugating $\Phi$ , we may assume that $h\left(f_{i}\right)\leq M\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f_{i}\right),1\right\}$ for some constant $M>0$ depending only on $d$ . Then our corollary follows from applying [69, Theorem 1.1] along with Theorem 1.5. ∎

We can now handle the general case of subvarieties $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ .

#### Proposition 8.7.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible subvariety of degree $D$ that is not preperiodic. Then there exists $E=E\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that $\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ is contained in a proper Zariski closed subvariety $W$ of degree at most $E$ .

#### Proof.

We induct on $n$ . Hence we may assume that $V$ projects dominantly to all its coordinates axes. Let $\dim V=r$ . If $V$ is not preperiodic, then as explained in the proof of [47, Proposition 2.1], there exists $r+1$ many coordinates and a projection $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{r+1}$ such that the image $\pi\left(V\right)$ is a non-preperiodic hypersurface. Note that the degree of $\pi$ when restricted to $V$ is bounded in terms of $D$ . Then if $W^{\prime}$ is a proper Zariski closed subvariety of $\pi\left(V\right)$ that contains all preperiodic points of $\pi\left(V\right)$ it follows that $W=\pi^{-1}(W^{\prime})$ is a proper closed subvariety of $V$ that contains all preperiodic points of $V$ . As $\deg W$ is bounded in terms of $\deg W^{\prime}$ and $D$ , it suffices to prove our Proposition for $\pi\left(V\right)$ .

After rearranging the coordinates, we may assume that $\pi$ is the projection to the first $r+1$ coordinates. Now if $\pi\left(V\right)$ is not weakly $\Phi^{\prime}$ -special for $\Phi^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r+1})$ , then Proposition 8.6 implies that we are done. Else $\pi\left(V\right)$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special. Since it project dominantly to all coordinates, we are left with the case where $\pi(V)=\pi^{\prime-1}(V^{\prime})$ for some projection $\pi^{\prime}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n-1}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n-2}$ . Then $\pi\left(V\right)$ is of the form $V^{\prime}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . As $V^{\prime}$ is not preperiodic, we are done by induction as desired. ∎

A simple induction gives uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford on $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ when at most one coordinate map is exceptional.

#### Corollary 8.8.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible subvariety of degree $D$ . Then there exists $N=N\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \overline{\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)}^{\operatorname{Zar}}\text{ is a union of at most }N\text{ preperiodic irreducible subvarieties.} $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately by induction from Proposition 8.7. ∎

## 9. Specialization from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$

The main results of this section are Theorems 1.4, 1.2 and 1.3 over $\mathbb{C}$ .

#### Theorem 9.1.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree and let $K=k\left(B\right)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve over $B$ . Assume that $k$ is of characteristic $0$ . Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{K}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible subvariety of degree $D$ . Then there exists $N=N\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \overline{\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\overline{K}\right)}^{\operatorname{Zar}}\text{ is a union of at most }N\text{ preperiodic irreducible subvarieties.} $$

To see why Theorem 9.1 implies the situation over $\mathbb{C}$ , we use the following proposition.

#### Proposition 9.2.

Let $K$ be a finitely generated extension of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ of positive transcendence degree. Then there exists $k\subset K$ such that $k$ is algebraically closed in $K$ and $K=k\left(B\right)$ for some geometrically irreducible projective curve $B$ over $k$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\operatorname{trdeg}K=n$ . Then we pick $n-1$ algebraically independent elements $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}$ and let $k=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})$ . Replacing $k$ with its algebraic closure inside $K$ , we obtain that $K$ is of transcendence degree $1$ over $k$ . Since $K$ is finitely generated over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , it is finitely generated over $k$ . Thus $K$ is a finite extension of $k(t)$ for any $t\in K$ transcendental over $k$ . It follows from [7, Lemma 1.4.10] that $K=k\left(B\right)$ for some irreducible projective curve $B$ over $k$ . Since $k$ is algebraically closed in $K$ and the characteristic is zero, the extension $K/k$ is regular. Hence $B$ is geometrically irreducible as desired. ∎

Our strategy to prove Theorem 9.1 follows the deduction of the uniform geometric Bogomolov conjecture for characteristic $0$ from the case of number fields by Mavraki and the second author [69]. If $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ is an endomorphism over $\mathbb{C}$ and $V$ a subvariety of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ , then we may find some $K$ so that $K$ is finitely generated over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for which $\Phi$ and $V$ are well-defined over. Using Proposition 9.2, we may write $K=k\left(B\right)$ for some smooth projective curve $B$ over $k$ with $k$ algebraically closed in $K$ . We can extend by scalars to replace $k$ with $\overline{k}$ to assume that $k$ is algebraically closed. Then Theorem 9.1 implies the number of irreducible components of $\overline{\operatorname{Prep}(\Phi)\cap V(\mathbb{C})}^{\operatorname{Zar}}$ is bounded above by $N$ as desired.

To prove Theorem 9.1, it suffices to prove the analogue of Proposition 8.7 over $K=k\left(B\right)$ . This will in turn follow from the analogue of Theorem 1.5, which we will state now. Note that as we have fixed ample height functions $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}$ and $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}$ , these naturally extend to height functions on $K$ -points for all characteristic zero function fields.

#### Proposition 9.3.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree and let $K=k\left(B\right)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve over $B$ . Assume that $k$ is of characteristic $0$ . Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{K}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at least one $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. Let $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible hypersurface of degree $D$ that is not weakly $\Phi$ -special. Then there exists $c=c\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)\geq ch_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right). $$

#### Proof.

We will proceed by induction on $\operatorname{trdeg}K$ . Let’s first handle the case where $k=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . We spread out $H$ as a flat family of hypersurfaces $\cal{H}_{t}$ over $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}\times U$ . We may also assume that $\Phi$ spreads out as a family of endomorphisms $\Phi_{t}$ over $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}\times U$ . Shrinking $U$ , we may also assume that every $f_{i,t}$ has degree $d$ and that $f_{i,t}$ is non-exceptional whenever $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. We now apply Silverman’s specialization theorem [69, Proposition 6.2]. The statement in [69] only applies to abelian varieties but the proof handles the dynamical setting too. We thus obtain

$$ \lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\\
h(t)\to\infty\end{subarray}}\frac{\widehat{h}_{\Phi_{t}}(\cal{H}_{t})}{h(t)}=\widehat{h}_{\Phi}(H). $$

Now we may assume that not all $f_{i}$ are isotrivial as else $\widehat{h}_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right)=0$ and there is nothing to prove. By Lemma 9.4, as $H$ is not weakly $\Phi$ -special, for some constant $C>0$ , there are only finitely many $t\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that $\cal{H}_{t}$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special and $h(t)>C$ . For $\cal{H}_{t}$ not weakly special, we obtain

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi_{t}}\left(\cal{H}_{t}\right)\geq ch_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi_{t}\right) $$

for $c>0$ depending only on $\left(d,n,D\right)$ . By Silverman’s specialization again, we know that

$$ \lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\\
h(t)\to\infty\end{subarray}}\frac{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\Phi_{t})}{h(t)}=h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\Phi) $$

and so (9.1) implies that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)\geq ch_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right) $$

as desired. For the general case, we first replace $k$ with a finitely generated extension over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for which $\Phi$ and $H$ are defined over. By Proposition 9.2, we may then write $k=k^{\prime}\left(B^{\prime}\right)$ for $k^{\prime}$ algebraically closed in $k$ and $B^{\prime}$ a smooth projective curve over $k^{\prime}$ . After extending scalars, we may assume that $k^{\prime}$ is algebraically closed. Since $\operatorname{trdeg}\left(k\right)<\operatorname{trdeg}\left(K\right)$ , by induction we know that Proposition 9.3 holds for $k=k^{\prime}\left(B^{\prime}\right)$ . Then the same argument as in the case of $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\left(B\right)$ implies that Proposition 9.3 for $k$ implies Proposition 9.3 for $K=k\left(B\right)$ since [69, Proposition 6.2] works for any $K=k\left(B\right)$ where $B$ is a curve over $k$ and $k$ is any function field. ∎

#### Lemma 9.4.

Assume that not all $f_{i}$ are isotrivial. If $H$ is not weakly $\Phi$ -special, there does not exist a sequence $t_{n}\in U\left(k\right)$ with $h(t_{n})\to\infty$ such that $\cal{H}_{t_{n}}$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special.

#### Proof.

Since $H$ projects dominantly to each coordinate, clearly $\cal{H}_{t}$ does so for $t$ in a Zariski open $V$ of $U$ . Now if there is a projection $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ so that $\cal{H}_{t}=\pi^{-1}(W_{t})$ for infinitely many $t$ , then viewing $\cal{H}$ as a hypersurface inside $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}\times B$ , we have $\cal{H}_{t}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times W_{t}\times\{t\}$ . Let $T$ be the set of such $t$ ’s and let $W$ be the Zariski closure of $\cup_{t\in T}\cal{H}_{t}$ . Then $W\subseteq\cal{H}$ and $\dim W\geq n$ . As we may assume that $\cal{H}$ is irreducible after shrinking $U$ , it follows that $W=\cal{H}$ . Then clearly $H$ is of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times W^{\prime}$ for some $W^{\prime}$ which contradicts $H$ being not weakly $\Phi$ -special.

If $n>2$ , a preperiodic fiber $\cal{H}_{t}$ would have a Zariski dense set of preperiodic points. Since it projects dominantly onto every collection of $n-1$ coordinates, [47, Theorem 2.2], together with [67], would force every $f_{i,t}$ to be exceptional. This contradicts the presence of a non-exceptional coordinate. Hence none of these fibers is weakly special. If $n=2$ , then we will show that if $\cal{H}_{t}$ is preperiodic for $\Phi_{t}$ for infinitely many $t$ , then $H$ itself is preperiodic for $\Phi$ . Each $\cal{H}_{t_{j}}$ must then be $\Phi_{t_{j}}$ -preperiodic, since at least one specialized map is non-exceptional and both projections of the curve are dominant. By the analogue of (9.1), we obtain that $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}(H)=0$ . We may now apply [68, Theorems 4.1 and 4.3]. Both these theorems work over general function fields of a curve. Since not both $f_{1},f_{2}$ are isotrivial, we must have that $H$ is $\Phi$ -preperiodic which contradicts $H$ being not weakly $\Phi$ -special as desired. ∎

We can now deduce the analogue of Proposition 8.7.

#### Proposition 9.5.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree and let $K=k\left(B\right)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve over $B$ . Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{K}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible subvariety of degree $D$ that is not preperiodic. Then there exists $E=E\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ such that $\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\overline{K}\right)$ is contained in a proper Zariski closed subvariety $W$ of degree at most $E$ .

#### Proof.

We again proceed by induction on $n$ and on $\operatorname{trdeg}K$ . The hypothesis that at most one coordinate map is exceptional is preserved under coordinate projections. Hence we may assume that $V$ projects dominantly to all coordinates. As in Proposition 8.7, since $V$ is not preperiodic, we may find a projection $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{r+1}$ where $r=\dim V$ such that the image $\pi\left(V\right)$ is a non-preperiodic hypersurface. After rearranging, we may assume that this is the first $r+1$ coordinates. Let’s first say that $\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r+1}\right)$ are not all isotrivial so that $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\Phi)>0$ . Then if $\pi\left(V\right)$ is not weakly $\Phi$ -special, applying Proposition 9.3 along with [69, Theorem 1.1] gives us the existence of a proper Zariski closed subvariety $W$ containing all points of canonical height $0$ with $\deg W$ bounded above by $E=E\left(d,n,D\right)>0$ . If $\pi\left(V\right)$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special, then it is of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times W$ for some $W\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{r}$ after rearranging coordinates. We are then done by induction again.

Now if $f_{1},\ldots,f_{r+1}$ are all isotrivial, we may conjugate them so that each $f_{i}$ are defined over $k$ . Then $\widehat{h}_{\Phi^{\prime}}$ for $\Phi^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r+1})$ is simply the standard Weil height $h$ . If $h\left(\pi\left(V\right)\right)>0$ , then applying [69, Theorem 1.1] again gives us our $W$ and $E$ . Else if $h\left(\pi\left(V\right)\right)=0$ , then $\pi\left(V\right)$ must itself must be defined over $k$ . Writing $k=k^{\prime}\left(B^{\prime}\right)$ with $B^{\prime}$ smooth projective over $k^{\prime}$ and $k^{\prime}$ algebraically closed in $k$ , we obtain our $W$ and $E$ by induction as $\operatorname{trdeg}k<\operatorname{trdeg}K$ . This finishes our proof. ∎

We recall the definition of special curves from [68].

#### Definition 9.6.

Let $f,g$ be rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ and let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be an irreducible curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ . We say that $C$ is $\left(f,g\right)$ -special if it is $\left(f,g\right)$ -preperiodic or if case (3) of Definition 7.1 holds with $H$ a torsion coset, i.e. a translate of a connected algebraic subgroup by a torsion point.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Suppose that $C$ is not $(f,g)$ -special. If at least one of $f,g$ is non-exceptional, we can then apply Theorem 1.4 with $n=2$ . A horizontal or vertical non-special curve contains no preperiodic points. We may therefore assume that both projections are dominant and both maps are exceptional.

Choose standard group presentations $\varphi_{i}:G_{i}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of degrees $k_{i}\leq 6$ : the degrees are $1$ for power maps, $2$ for Chebyshev maps, and $2,3,4$ or $6$ for Lattès maps; see [71, Section 2 and Theorem 3.1]. Let $G:=G_{1}\times G_{2}$ , $\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2})$ and $Y=\varphi^{-1}(C)$ . The degree of $Y$ (in the standard compactification of $G$ ) is uniformly bounded by a number depending only on $D$ .

Applying [52, Theorem 1.1] to $Y$ and the rank-zero torsion subgroup $G_{\mathrm{tors}}$ , we can bound $\#(Y\cap G_{\mathrm{tors}})$ only in terms of $D$ .

Every preperiodic point in $C\cap\operatorname{Im}\varphi$ lifts to a torsion point of $G$ . Each $\varphi_{i}$ omits at most two points of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , so $C\setminus\operatorname{Im}\varphi$ contains at most $2D$ points. Combining these bounds proves the theorem. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let $\Delta\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be the diagonal. If $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\neq\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ , then [4, Theorem 1.2] implies that $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ is finite. Thus $\Delta$ is not $(f,g)$ -special. Applying Theorem 1.2 to $\Delta$ , we have

$$ \left|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)\right|=\left|\Delta\cap\operatorname{Prep}(f,g)\right|\leq B(d,2), $$

which finishes the proof. ∎
